paragraphs: Rabbi Avin bar Bisna: [Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 1:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yevamot.1.1.24).
Rabbi Chinena bar Bisna. Hyman cites Ketubot 110a; compare [Beitzah 22a](https://www.sefaria.org/Beitzah.22a.5).
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna. Hyman cites Shabbat 106a; compare [Avodah Zarah 33b](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.33b.5).
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna. Hyman cites Ketubot 110a; compare [Niddah 42a](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.42a.4).[^3]

notes.text: The Midrash Rabbah — TE digital Bereshit Rabbah 18:1 has Rabbi Elazar bar Bisna, whereas Hyman supplies Eliezer. The returned research did not locate the Chinena and Shmuel notices at Ketubot 110a or the Yitzchak notice at Shabbat 106a; these three units remain held without claiming absence from the works.

Hyman’s printed entry (vol. I, p. 267) gives the five references as recorded here. In the Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot 1:1, Guggenheimer’s edition reads Rabbi Abun bar Bisna. Bereshit Rabbah 18:1 reads Elazar, as noted above. The consulted Babylonian Talmud has Rav Chinena bar Bisna in Beitzah 22a, Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna in Avodah Zarah 33b, and Rav Shmuel bar Bisna in Niddah 42a. These passages supply the additional evidence for the three notices discussed in the preceding note. Hyman’s citations to Ketubot 110a and Shabbat 106a remain unverified. The shared patronymic supplies no further identification.

[Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 1:1:24](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yevamot.1.1.24) names Abun bar Bisna, and [Bereshit Rabbah 18:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.18.1) names Elazar bar Bisna. The parallel [Seder HaDorot list](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=707&lang=en) gives Avin, Chinena, Yitzchak and Shmuel among its patronymics. The passages leave the relationships among these names open.
